The Scottis
The 1955 Le Mans disaster had changed Euro-
pean motor racing overnight. Mercedes-Benz had
withdrawn from racing, and countries such as Swit-
zerland had banned circuit racing altogether. Alt-
hough
Mike Hawthorn was listed as the 1955 winner in
his Jaguar D-Type, his pit entry manoeuvre had
also caused an accident that claimed the lives of
84 people and highlighted that the French circuit
was no longer up to the task of handling such fast
cars. Work on a completely new pitlane, speed-re-
ducing chicanes approaching the pits and track wi-
dening took 13 months before the traditional race
was started in July 1956, though this time without
World Championship status.
Jaguar D-Type Ecurie Ecosse Winner Le Mans 1956
Ninian Sanderson, Ron Flockhart
Spark 1/18th, 20-18056, € 220,00
Memoria
Ron Flockhart had joined Ecurie Ecosse for the
1956 season and lined up alongside his compatri-
ot Ninian Sanderson in the privateer Jaguar D-Type.
Two Scots in a Scottish team, proudly displaying
their national colours of blue and white on the Bri-
tish car.
Whether it was down to the pouring rain, the nu-
merous accidents or the fact that the competitors
from Aston Martin and Ferrari were fielding cars
with only 2.5-litre engines is impossible to say 70
years on. In the history books, anyway, the success
of David Murray’s private team occupies a special
place, surpassed only by the Scottish one-two vic-
tory with the D-Type the following year.

Japanese Near-Sensation
Whilst the Japanese Maki Team was already dis-
banding at the famous 1976 F1 season finale at
Fuji, a new Japanese team appeared in the pad-
dock in the form of Kojima. The KEO07 had been
designed by former Maki engineer Masao Ono. It
was very well built and, thanks to its sophisticated
aerodynamics, showed considerable potential.
The competition was quite astonished when Ma-
sahiro Hasemi emerged in fourth place in the first
practice session. During second practice, he was
even on course to beat Mario Andretti’s later pole
time in the Lotus when a suspension component
snapped whilst braking for the final corner, dama-
ging the car.
In qualifying, the black newcomer still managed to
secure 10th on the grid - ahead of 16 other cars
from Lotus, Ligier, McLaren, Tyrrell and Brabham!
Ultimately, it was the team’s inexperience that
prevented a top finish in the race. The Kojima had
been built solely for this one appearance, tuned
specifically for the circuit at Mount Fuji.
A full Formula 1 season had never been the team’s
objective. But what might have happened if the Ko-
jima had actually started the race from pole posi-
tion? As it stands, all that remains is the thrilling
story of a near-sensation at the home Grand Prix -
one that was not to be repeated during the second
and final attempt in 1977.
Kojima KEO07 Ford Cosworth F1 11° Japanese GP 1976
Masahiro Hasemi
